sentences.text: Based on fragmentary fossils, Ajkaceratops was estimated to have a body length of 1 meter.
Ajkaceratops fossils represent the first discovery of this dinosaur group in Europe.
The genus Ajkaceratops was described in 2010.
The genus name honors the Hungarian town of Ajka where the fossils were found and the Greek word for horned face.
The holotype specimen MTM V2009.192.1 consists of a few skull fragments including the snout, fused premaxillae, and maxillae fragments.
The Ajkaceratops fossils are housed in the Hungarian Natural History Museum in Budapest.
New remains of Ajkaceratops kozmai were found in the Late Cretaceous Csehbánya Formation in Hungary, according to Maidment et al. (2026).
This animal processed its food by moving its jaws in a circular pattern.
When first described, Ajkaceratops was considered most similar to the Asian protoceratopsid Bagaceratops.
Later research questioned Ajkaceratops's classification as a ceratopsian because its proposed rostral bone has a sub-circular cross-section and pitted texture unlike other ceratopsians.
In 2026, a more complete skull specimen supported the classification of Ajkaceratops as a ceratopsian.
Ajkaceratops belongs to the parent group Ceratopsia.
Ajkaceratops is classified in the class Ornithischia.
Ajkaceratops lived during the Late Cretaceous in the western Tethyan archipelago, which is now part of Europe.
Ajkaceratops lived during the Santonian stage, approximately 86 to 84 million years ago.
Ajkaceratops fossils were found in the Csehbánya Formation, interpreted as a floodplain and channel deposit made of clay, silt, sand, and sandstone.
Ajkaceratops shared its environment with Rhabdodon, nodosaurids, non-avian theropods, enantiornithine birds, eusuchian crocodilians, azhdarchid pterosaurs, Bothremydidae turtles, and teiid lizards.
It is debated whether Ajkaceratops is a unique ceratopsian or an enigmatic ornithischian with uncertain affinities.
Some studies based on the premaxilla reinterpretation suggest Ajkaceratops is a basal ornithopod, specifically the sister taxon to Changmiania.
